Do not give a dose.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"LactMed reports the following for amoxicillin in breastfed infants:\\n\\n**Measured exposure**\\n\\n- In milk samples from 6 women, average amoxicillin concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** (range **0.46\u20130.88 mg/L**) at 4 hours and **0.81 mg/L** (range **0.39\u20131.3 mg/L**) at 5 hours after administration. These are **milk concentrations**, not infant-level measurements. Relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the LactMed record\u2019s revision date. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n- LactMed\u2019s record does not establish a numeric study count from the extract.\\n\\n**Observed infant symptoms**\\n\\n- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 reported diarrhea in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a prospective study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breast milk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. The cited study concerns amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and cefuroxime during lactation. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- A study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with infants exposed to a macrolide reported adverse reactions in 8.3% of the amoxicillin-exposed infants, including rash and somnolence; the rate was similar in the comparison group. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- One case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a 2-month-old after breastfeeding while the mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and gentamicin. The report could not determine which drug caused the reaction; LactMed judged the combination product the more likely cause. [S3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- In another report, an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin with acetaminophen plus codeine experienced mild diarrhea. The attribution was rated possible or probable. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of 25 mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. This is a reported study finding, not proof that adverse effects cannot occur. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n**Advice to monitor**\\n\\n- The retrieved LactMed text does **not give a separate recommendation** for an individual to monitor a particular symptom.\\n- One study asked mothers to monitor for tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, and skin rash; weight change and jaundice were also recorded. Those were **study-measured items**, not evidence that each symptom occurred or a general monitoring recommendation. [S21](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\n**Uncertainty**\\n\\nLactMed states that rash and possible gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea or thrush have been reported, but that these effects have not been adequately evaluated. The reports differ in their populations, methods, comparison groups, co-exposures, and\u2014where applicable\u2014whether the product was amoxicillin alone or amoxicillin/clavulanate. The case report does not establish causation. The retrieved record contains all expected sections without truncation, but it is still a bounded extract and its study count is not established; missing information is not evidence of safety. [S21](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nThe LactMed copy was published in an NCBI package dated October 22, 2026, and the record was revised June 15, 2026; the record link should be checked for newer changes. [S4](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv) Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; discuss changes with the prescribing clinician.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
LactMed reports the following for amoxicillin in breastfed infants:

**Measured exposure**

- In milk samples from 6 women, average amoxicillin concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** (range **0.46–0.88 mg/L**) at 4 hours and **0.81 mg/L** (range **0.39–1.3 mg/L**) at 5 hours after administration. These are **milk concentrations**, not infant-level measurements. Relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the LactMed record’s revision date. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)
- LactMed’s record does not establish a numeric study count from the extract.

**Observed infant symptoms**

- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 reported diarrhea in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a prospective study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breast milk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. The cited study concerns amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and cefuroxime during lactation. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- A study comparing amoxicillin-exposed infants with infants exposed to a macrolide reported adverse reactions in 8.3% of the amoxicillin-exposed infants, including rash and somnolence; the rate was similar in the comparison group. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- One case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a 2-month-old after breastfeeding while the mother was receiving amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and gentamicin. The report could not determine which drug caused the reaction; LactMed judged the combination product the more likely cause. [S3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- In another report, an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin with acetaminophen plus codeine experienced mild diarrhea. The attribution was rated possible or probable. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of 25 mothers and infants older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. This is a reported study finding, not proof that adverse effects cannot occur. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

**Advice to monitor**

- The retrieved LactMed text does **not give a separate recommendation** for an individual to monitor a particular symptom.
- One study asked mothers to monitor for tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool changes, diaper rash, and skin rash; weight change and jaundice were also recorded. Those were **study-measured items**, not evidence that each symptom occurred or a general monitoring recommendation. [S21](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

**Uncertainty**

LactMed states that rash and possible gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea or thrush have been reported, but that these effects have not been adequately evaluated. The reports differ in their populations, methods, comparison groups, co-exposures, and—where applicable—whether the product was amoxicillin alone or amoxicillin/clavulanate. The case report does not establish causation. The retrieved record contains all expected sections without truncation, but it is still a bounded extract and its study count is not established; missing information is not evidence of safety. [S21](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

The LactMed copy was published in an NCBI package dated October 22, 2026, and the record was revised June 15, 2026; the record link should be checked for newer changes. [S4](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv) Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; discuss changes with the prescribing clinician.

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
### Measured exposure

LactMed reports **sumatriptan concentrations in breast milk**:

- One study reported a peak milk concentration averaging **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), measured about **2.5 hours** after administration in five breastfeeding women. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/)
- Another study reported peak milk concentrations averaging **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**), occurring **2–4 hours** after administration. The average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**). [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

These are **milk-exposure measurements**. They are not measurements of an infant’s specimen.

### What was observed in infants

LactMed states that relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the record’s revision date. It reports manufacturer correspondence describing **three breastfeeding women** who used sumatriptan; none reported adverse effects in their infants. The exposure amounts and routes were unspecified. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

Thus, the milk concentrations and the infant observations are different evidence: the former measures drug presence in milk, while the latter is a small, indirectly reported observation about infant outcomes. It does not provide measured infant levels or establish that effects were absent in all infants. The LactMed extract is a bounded record; its study count was not established from the extract, and absence of a retrieved infant-level measurement is not evidence of safety. The MCP also notes that changing medication can carry risks and that this lookup cannot determine an individual treatment plan.

Application limits:
This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.

Its **Warnings** section describes lactic acidosis as a rare, serious complication and discusses contexts including renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, certain heart-failure contexts, older age, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, and excessive alcohol intake. It also lists other reported reactions, including hypoglycemia, dyspnea, rash, and headache. These are findings in the medicine-taker population, not breastfed infants. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\nIn its lactation section, the label states that animal studies found metformin excreted into milk, that comparable studies had not been conducted in nursing mothers, and that potential hypoglycemia in nursing infants was a concern. This is a label warning or uncertainty statement, not an observed infant outcome. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\n### Breastfed-infant evidence\\n\\nLactMed reports measured milk and infant-level concentrations and separately describes observed infant outcomes. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\n**Measured exposure**\\n\\n- **Milk concentrations:** average **270 mcg/L** in one group; approximately **380 mcg/L** in one sample collected about 4\u20135 hours after administration.\\n- **Milk concentrations:** averages of **130 and 270 mcg/L** in two women over the following 72 hours.\\n- **Milk concentrations:** averages of **130\u2013270 mcg/L** in three mothers.\\n- **Milk concentrations:** average **410 mcg/L** when trough and peak milk samples were collected 4\u201317 days postpartum.\\n- **Infant serum:** measurements were retrieved for four breastfed infants. These concentrations are research measurements, not medication doses or treatment instructions. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n- The selected DailyMed product was not confirmed to match the exact formulation being taken. request.question: Compare metformin label warnings for the adult taking it with findings in breastfed infants. Identify which source says what, and disclose missing sections. Don't give any doses.

response.answer:
## Metformin: adult label warnings compared with breastfed-infant findings

### Adult medicine-taker label

The retrieved DailyMed label is for **METFORMIN HCL TABLET [QPHARMA, INC.]**. The product/formulation match to a particular patient’s medicine was not confirmed. Its **Warnings** section describes lactic acidosis as a rare, serious complication and discusses contexts including renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, certain heart-failure contexts, older age, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, and excessive alcohol intake. The retrieved warning text is truncated. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s **Adverse Reactions** section reports gastrointestinal reactions—including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort—in adults with type 2 diabetes. It also lists other reported reactions, including hypoglycemia, dyspnea, rash, and headache. These are findings in the medicine-taker population, not breastfed infants. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

In its lactation section, the label states that animal studies found metformin excreted into milk, that comparable studies had not been conducted in nursing mothers, and that potential hypoglycemia in nursing infants was a concern. This is a label warning or uncertainty statement, not an observed infant outcome. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

### Breastfed-infant evidence

LactMed reports measured milk and infant-level concentrations and separately describes observed infant outcomes. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

**Measured exposure**

- **Milk concentrations:** average **270 mcg/L** in one group; approximately **380 mcg/L** in one sample collected about 4–5 hours after administration.
- **Milk concentrations:** averages of **130 and 270 mcg/L** in two women over the following 72 hours.
- **Milk concentrations:** averages of **130–270 mcg/L** in three mothers.
- **Milk concentrations:** average **410 mcg/L** when trough and peak milk samples were collected 4–17 days postpartum.
- **Infant serum:** measurements were retrieved for four breastfed infants. Two were undetectable at **<10 mcg/L**; two had levels of **50 and 80 mcg/L** at the reported sampling times.
- **Infant serum:** metformin was undetectable at **<5 mcg/L** in two additional infants whose levels were measured.

The retrieved LactMed record does not provide the ages or extent of nursing for some infants with measured levels. These concentrations are research measurements, not medication doses or treatment instructions. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

**Observed infant outcomes**

- LactMed reports seven infants aged 5–25 months judged healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two also had normal Denver developmental screening results.
- Three infants had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin.
- In three breastfed infants 10–11 days postpartum, none had low blood glucose, and their mothers reported no adverse reactions.
- In a study involving 111 infants—61 predominantly breastfed and 50 formula-fed—no differences were found in reported 3- and 6-month height, weight, motor-social development, or illness rates between the groups.

These are the outcomes reported in the cited LactMed summaries; they do not convert the adult label warning into an infant outcome. The LactMed extract does not establish a total study count. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/) [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16737874/)

### Comparison

| Topic | Adult label | Breastfed-infant evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Lactic acidosis | Described as a serious warning for the medicine taker, with specified clinical risk contexts. | No lactic-acidosis outcome is reported in the retrieved LactMed infant-outcome section; this silence does not establish that it was absent from all evidence. |
| Hypoglycemia | Listed among adult adverse reactions; the lactation section also raises potential infant hypoglycemia as a concern. | One LactMed study reports no low blood glucose in three infants and no reported infant adverse reactions in that study. |
| Gastrointestinal effects | Adult label reports diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, and abdominal discomfort. | These effects are not reported as observed infant outcomes in the retrieved LactMed extract. |
| Drug exposure | The label concerns the medicine-taker population. | LactMed reports measured milk concentrations and infant serum concentrations separately from clinical outcomes. |

### Missing and retrieval limitations

- The DailyMed **Warnings** section is truncated.
- **Warnings and Precautions** and **Boxed Warning** were not retrieved from the selected label; their absence from this extract does not prove absence from the full labeling. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- The selected DailyMed product was not confirmed to match the exact formulation being taken. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- LactMed returned its four expected sections without truncation or omission, but its total study count is not established from the extract; reference count is not study count. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)
- LactMed’s record was revised August 15, 2026, and the retrieved record is a saved copy from an NCBI package published October 22, 2026; the record link should be checked for later changes. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

request.question: Search FDA recall records for naproxen. The fictional bottle lot is NOTREAL-77. If the lot is not found, can the lookup establish that the bottle was unaffected? Explain what still needs verification.

This **does not establish that the bottle was unaffected**: the lookup is not bottle-level clearance, and the returned assessment is “not found in text—not clearance.” [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/enforcement.json?search=product_description%3A%22naproxen%22&sort=report_date%3Adesc&limit=20)

### What still needs verification

Verify the bottle’s:

- exact product and formulation;
- manufacturer, distributor, or repackager;
- lot number, including possible printing or transcription differences;
- expiration date;
- NDC, UPC, package size, and labeling;
- correspondence with the complete official recall notice.

The lookup’s limitations state that candidate product-name matches are not bottle-level clearance; a no-match, different lot, or terminated recall does not prove the product safe; and lot ranges or all-lot notices require human interpretation. request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes—an FDA directory listing was returned for topiramate:

- **Registry:** The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry  
- **Listed products:** Topamax, Trokendi XR, Qudexy XR (topiramate)  
- **Conditions listed:** Epilepsy, mood disorder, migraine headaches  
- **Status as listed:** Ongoing  
- **Contact:** Massachusetts General Hospital for Children; toll-free phone **1-888-233-2334**  
- **Enrollment link:** [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)  
- **FDA directory listing:** [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

This is a registry listing, not a determination that any particular person is eligible to enroll. The registry team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. The FDA directory states that it does not operate or endorse the registries and that its list is not comprehensive. The lookup did not establish the registry’s source population or age band.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find up to two recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States. Include exact study links, overall and site status if present, update dates, contacts and qualification limits. Do not decide whether a child qualifies.

response.answer:
## Recruiting U.S. ADHD studies involving children

The search returned two potential matches. Both records are listed as **interventional** studies; the registry’s source-population field says **“not established”** for both. These are directory listings, not eligibility determinations. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Virtual-reality interventions for ADHD — NCT05608434

**Exact study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05608434)

- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **U.S. site status:** NIH Clinical Center, Bethesda, Maryland — RECRUITING
- **Last update posted:** 2026-11-12
- **Age listed:** 8–16 years; the pilot is listed as ages 10–16.
- **Qualification limits listed:** Parent consent and child assent; ADHD diagnosis or a specified impairing inattention presentation; ability to complete study procedures and travel to the NIH Clinical Center. The record also lists cognitive, neurological, visual, psychiatric, medical, prior cognitive-training, and study-procedure exclusions. The pilot and main trial have different medication-related requirements.
- **Contacts:**  
  - Saadia A. Choudhury — (301) 437-0489 — saadia.choudhury@nih.gov  
  - Daniel S. Pine, M.D. — (301) 594-1318 — daniel.pine@nih.gov  
  - NIH Clinical Center Office of Patient Recruitment — 800-411-1222 — ccopr@nih.gov

### 2. SPN-812 (viloxazine extended-release) in preschool-age children with ADHD — NCT04781140

**Exact study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04781140)

- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **Last update posted:** 2026-10-05
- **Age listed:** 48–69 months.
- **Site statuses:** The returned record includes RECRUITING, WITHDRAWN, and TERMINATED U.S. sites. The location list is truncated, so it is not a complete site list.
- **Qualification limits listed:** Parent/legal-guardian consent; primary ADHD diagnosis confirmed through structured assessment; specified symptom-severity criteria; participation in a structured group activity; behavioral-treatment and medication-related requirements; and medical, neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular, dietary, investigational-drug, and other exclusion criteria.
- **Central contact:** Olivia Elbaum — 301-838-2500 — clinicaltrials@supernus.com
- **Returned recruiting-site contacts include:**  
  - The Center for Clinical Trials, Saraland, Alabama — 251-341-7021 — info@thecenterforclinicaltrials.com  
  - Preferred Research Partners, Little Rock, Arkansas — 501-553-9987 — info@preferredresearchpartners.com  
  - Advanced Research Center, Anaheim, California — 714-999-6688 — contact@arctrials.com  
  - Sun Valley Research Center, Imperial, California — 760-545-0123 — svrcinfo@sunvalleyb.com  
  - Alliance Research, Long Beach, California — 562-548-8500 — Research@asclepes.com  
  - Clinical Neuroscience Solutions, Jacksonville, Florida — 904-281-5757  
  - Avantis Clinical Research, Miami, Florida — 305-515-9006 — info@avantisclinicalresearch.com

The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability; this lookup does not determine either. The search was bounded to the first 20 API matches and used literal ADHD/child matching, so it was not exhaustive. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One **RECRUITING** pediatric study was returned for Canada:

### Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics
- **Study type:** Observational  
- **Registry status:** RECRUITING  
- **Source population:** Children aged 3–17 years; the registry summary states that the study follows children with authorizations for medical cannabis across Canada.  
- **Epilepsy relevance:** Epilepsy appears among the listed conditions. The match is marked **indirect_or_unverified**, and clinical suitability for an individual is not confirmed.  
- **Location:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba — site status: RECRUITING  
- **Study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)  
- **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD — 204-272-3149; lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca  

No second study was returned. Completed studies were not substituted. The search was bounded and used literal topic matching; synonyms may have been missed. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

A report describes a **suspected** medication problem; by itself, it does **not establish that the medicine caused it**. The retrieved resource is for reporting instructions, not emergency care. No report was filed and no identifying information was requested.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* (2022)  
**PMID:** 34131926 [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Study design/methods:** A formal design label was not stated in the abstract. The reported methods involved breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam who completed a questionnaire. Researchers measured levetiracetam in serial breast-milk samples from pre-dose through 12 hours post-dose and in one pre-dose maternal serum sample. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Population:** 20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. Ages, prematurity, and other detailed population characteristics were not provided in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Drug exposure:** The trough breast-milk/serum levetiracetam ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**. The abstract also reports correlations among maternal levetiracetam dose, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Observed infant outcomes:** Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants; the abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding. The abstract reports that all infants gained weight according to age. It does not establish that levetiracetam caused the somnolence, and it does not provide longer-term infant outcomes. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

The requested PubMed abstract was retrieved successfully; no records were missing or failed in that abstract lookup. The search itself was not a complete literature review.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
**Age scope queried:** FAERS reports coded for ages **0 through 12 months**, with age recorded in months. Other age-unit encodings were excluded; therefore, this does not cover all infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

### What the reports can tell researchers

They show the **reporting volume of reaction terms within this queried subset**. The returned terms included vomiting (**117 reports**), pyrexia (**98**), and rash (**60**). The returned source population and confirmed age band for these reaction categories were not established beyond the database filter. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

### What they cannot establish

- **How often side effects occur:** exposure denominators were unavailable, so these counts cannot calculate incidence or risk.
- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** the spontaneous reports do not establish causation.
- **Whether the findings apply to all infants or all exposed infants:** the queried results cannot be generalized to those populations.

The MCP identifies these as reporting-volume counts, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or proof of causation. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10) [S2](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

### Measured exposure

LactMed reported these **breastmilk** concentrations:

- Pooled analysis: sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L**. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)
- Twenty-six women sampled over 24 hours: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L**. Norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L**. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- Four mothers at 2 months postpartum: sertraline averaged **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L**, with samples collected at random times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, across three samples collected at random times. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk collected at 4 weeks postpartum contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively; sampling occurred 13 hours after administration. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In first-week postpartum trough samples, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in eight others. The source notes that timing could affect those values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Another study reported a median milk sertraline concentration of **11.3 mcg/L**, range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**; sampling was random, and the source notes that timing could affect accuracy. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Fifteen mothers had an average milk concentration of **87 mcg/L**, range **12–288 mcg/L**, with samples collected at specified times between just before administration and 14 hours afterward. [S42](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/)

The returned LactMed exposure extract did **not** include numeric infant-level concentrations. Its narrative states that infant serum sertraline is usually not detected and that low levels of norsertraline are often detectable, but the exact infant specimens and values were not available in the returned exposure-measurement excerpt. The “Drug Levels” section was truncated. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The returned LactMed extract reported:

- One 4-month-old infant had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 26 infants, no detectable acute adverse reactions were reported. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In a study of 14 mother–infant pairs, infant whole-blood serotonin averages were 227 mcg/L before and 224 mcg/L after maternal treatment; no adverse effects were reported in those infants. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- In a study of 25 infants, 6-month weight gain was reported as normal according to national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- Six infants aged 5–34 weeks had no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of the study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)
- Seven 4-week-old infants had no reported adverse effects. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/)
- In a study of infants exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and breastfeeding, four infants were exposed to sertraline. The study reported blunted pain responses in the exposed group; the comparison group did not include depressed, unmedicated mothers, so the source stated that an effect related to maternal depression could not be ruled out. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)
- A case report described a preterm infant born at 33 weeks with hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation problems, and high-pitched crying. The returned extract reports infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and states that the authors attributed the symptoms to serotonergic overstimulation in that case. This is a single case report. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)

The LactMed “Effects in Breastfed Infants” section was truncated, so additional outcome details were not available in the returned extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Product-label evidence

The selected DailyMed product is **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, SPL version 13, effective **November 5, 2026**. The lookup did not confirm that this is the exact product or formulation in use. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

Its lactation section states that published literature shows low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk. It reports a pooled analysis of **53 mother–infant pairs** in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to **2%** of maternal serum levels, with a range of **0%–15%**; no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. - In a case involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, across three samples collected at random times. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk collected at 4 weeks postpartum contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively; sampling occurred 13 hours after administration. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In first-week postpartum trough samples, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in eight others. The source notes that timing could affect those values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Another study reported a median milk sertraline concentration of **11.3 mcg/L**, range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**; sampling was random, and the source notes that timing could affect accuracy. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Fifteen mothers had an average milk concentration of **87 mcg/L**, range **12–288 mcg/L**, with samples collected at specified times between just before administration and 14 hours afterward. [S42](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/)

The returned LactMed exposure extract did **not** include numeric infant-level concentrations. request.question: Prepare an evidence brief for sertraline during lactation using the medication evidence brief tool. Include questions to ask my clinician, source links, and missing evidence limitations. Do not provide medication decisions or doses.

response.answer:
## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation

**Identity:** The lookup matched sertraline exactly. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

**Evidence status:** Evidence was retrieved, but the MCP result is partial and is not a safety verdict. LactMed’s Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated; the record should not be treated as complete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### 1. Effects on the lactating person

- LactMed reports galactorrhea case reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients and cites a pharmacovigilance analysis that did not find an increased hyperprolactinemia signal compared with other medicines. These findings do not directly establish an effect during established lactation. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A report described six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; administered regimens were not reported. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed label states that data on sertraline’s effects on milk production are unavailable. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### 2. Measured exposure

Retrieved milk-concentration measurements included:

- Sertraline **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 26 women, sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L**. Norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- At two months postpartum, mean milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline in four mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline; sampling times were random. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk concentrations at four weeks postpartum, 13 hours after exposure, were **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One milk measurement was **<5 mcg/L**; another study reported milk concentrations of **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In six women, the median milk concentration was **11.3 mcg/L**, with a range of **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**; the source notes that sampling timing might affect accuracy. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 15 mothers, the mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L**, range **12–288 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned LactMed exposure extract does not include a complete infant-level concentration section. A PubMed abstract reports detectable concentrations of sertraline in three nursing infants and desmethylsertraline in six; it describes the specimen as infant serum. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

These are research measurements, not dosing instructions. Milk concentrations do not establish safety.

### 3. Observed infant outcomes

The retrieved extract reports:

- One four-month-old infant had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A study of 26 infants reported no detectable acute adverse reactions. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Other small reports described no clinically noted adverse reactions or no adverse reactions requiring medical attention in the reported infants. These reports do not establish that unaddressed outcomes were absent. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A study involving 30 infants reported blunted pain responses among SSRI-exposed infants; four were exposed to sertraline. The source states that there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, so the contribution of maternal depression-related behavior was not resolved. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)[S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- An uncontrolled survey of 930 mothers reported infant drug-discontinuation symptoms in about 10% of infants; the extract does not make this finding sertraline-specific. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/)[S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A case involving a preterm infant born at 33 weeks reported hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation abnormalities, and high-pitched crying. The source also reports infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and describes the authors’ attribution to sertraline exposure through breastmilk in that case. This is a single case report, not a population estimate. [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)[S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Label context

The selected DailyMed label describes low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk and reports no observed adverse reactions in a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs. This is one selected product label, not all sertraline formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### FAERS report-only context

A general sertraline FAERS query returned:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhoea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

These are reports matching the query, not a complete exposed population. The returned population was not established as lactating or infant-specific. FAERS counts are reporting volume, not rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation; exposure denominators were unavailable. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)

### Literature and retrieval limitations

The PubMed query returned 129 records, but only five records were included in the bounded extract. Abstract text was retrieved for three:

- Abstract retrieved: PMID 12452737. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12452737/)
- Abstract retrieved: PMID 38811474. [S48](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/)
- Abstract retrieved: PMID 9286185. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- **No abstract text returned:** PMID 38133585. [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)
- **No abstract text returned:** PMID 32320387. [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the study or research does not exist. Titles alone were not used to summarize outcomes. The search was bounded and not a systematic review. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

### Questions to ask your clinician

The MCP-generated questions for discussion are:

- Does this evidence apply to my exact medicine, formulation, and all active ingredients?
- How closely do the study populations match the lactation context, including infant age and prematurity?
- Which findings measure exposure, and which measure clinical outcomes?
- What uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?
- What questions about benefits, risks, and follow-up should we address together?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice is: **Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.**

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Use the evidence brief tool.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Questions to ask your clinician\\n\\n- Does the evidence apply to my exact sertraline product, formulation, and other active ingredients? [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)\\n- How closely do the study populations match my breastfeeding situation, including my infant\u2019s age and whether my infant was premature?\\n- Which findings measure drug exposure, and which describe observed infant outcomes?\\n- What were the measured sertraline and norsertraline concentrations in breast milk, and how should those measurements be interpreted for my infant? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- Was infant-level information measured in the studies, and what specimen was used?\\n- How should the small studies, case reports, and incomplete evidence be weighed when discussing uncertainty? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- What is known about infant development and longer-term outcomes, and what remains unestablished in the retrieved evidence?\\n- Are there considerations specific to a premature infant or an infant with possible differences in drug metabolism? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- What maternal effects should we discuss separately from infant exposure, including the limited evidence concerning milk production? [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32) [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- How should my clinical need for treatment and the risks of changing treatment be considered alongside the breastfeeding evidence? [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n- What follow-up information about my infant would be relevant to discuss with you?\\n- Would a pharmacist with breastfeeding or perinatal-medicine expertise add useful input?\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nThe retrieved LactMed extract reports breast-milk concentrations including sertraline values of **45 mcg/L** (range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**), **129 mcg/L** (range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**), **26.4 mcg/L**, **201 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **58 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**), and **87 mcg/L** (range **12\u2013288 mcg/L**). Reported norsertraline concentrations included **258 mcg/L** (range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**), **29 mcg/L**, and **358 mcg/L**. Sampling contexts varied, including random times, trough samples, and a sample taken 13 hours after a dose. These are research concentrations, not individualized treatment instructions. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe LactMed extract states that infant-level information was retrieved in the broader record, but the numeric infant-level excerpt was **not present in the returned measurement field**. request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

- Does the evidence apply to my exact sertraline product, formulation, and other active ingredients? [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)
- How closely do the study populations match my breastfeeding situation, including my infant’s age and whether my infant was premature?
- Which findings measure drug exposure, and which describe observed infant outcomes?
- What were the measured sertraline and norsertraline concentrations in breast milk, and how should those measurements be interpreted for my infant? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Was infant-level information measured in the studies, and what specimen was used?
- How should the small studies, case reports, and incomplete evidence be weighed when discussing uncertainty? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- What is known about infant development and longer-term outcomes, and what remains unestablished in the retrieved evidence?
- Are there considerations specific to a premature infant or an infant with possible differences in drug metabolism? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- What maternal effects should we discuss separately from infant exposure, including the limited evidence concerning milk production? [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32) [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- How should my clinical need for treatment and the risks of changing treatment be considered alongside the breastfeeding evidence? [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- What follow-up information about my infant would be relevant to discuss with you?
- Would a pharmacist with breastfeeding or perinatal-medicine expertise add useful input?

### Measured exposure

The retrieved LactMed extract reports breast-milk concentrations including sertraline values of **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**), **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**), **26.4 mcg/L**, **201 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **58 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**), and **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**). Reported norsertraline concentrations included **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**), **29 mcg/L**, and **358 mcg/L**. Sampling contexts varied, including random times, trough samples, and a sample taken 13 hours after a dose. These are research concentrations, not individualized treatment instructions. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The LactMed extract states that infant-level information was retrieved in the broader record, but the numeric infant-level excerpt was **not present in the returned measurement field**. The Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections were truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Retrieval limitations

The PubMed search was bounded rather than systematic. Abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested records; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. This is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those studies or other research do not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

FAERS information was also retrieved separately. The returned query covered reports matching sertraline in the broad “any” cohort, not a confirmed breastfeeding population. The reported terms and counts included nausea **14,075**, drug ineffective **13,855**, fatigue **13,021**, headache **11,284**, anxiety **10,530**, diarrhoea **10,499**, dizziness **9,741**, and depression **9,612**. These are reporting volumes, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query does not establish causation or an exposure denominator. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice is that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.
PubMed abstract coverage: abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested PMIDs. No abstract text was returned for PMID(s): 38133585, 32320387. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that a study or research does not exist. Titles alone are not outcome evidence.

These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

The label states that no available data in pregnant women permit evaluation of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef)\\n\\n**Animal context, not human outcome evidence:** The label reports no fetal toxicity or malformation in the described rat and rabbit reproduction studies at the tested exposure levels. ## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** Lamotrigine was resolved as the single ingredient requested. [S25](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

**Scope:** Evidence was retrieved from one selected DailyMed product label and a bounded PubMed search. The PubMed search returned 690 records; seven requested abstracts were retrieved, with no failed or unreturned abstract lookups. This was not a systematic review. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S12](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29+AND+%28%22Pharmacokinetics%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Drug+Elimination+Routes%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pharmacokinetic%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+clearance%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22area+under+the+curve%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22dose+adjustment%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=3&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/) [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33573557/) [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35133310/) [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/) [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/) [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40593436/)

### 1. Effects on the pregnant person

The retrieved material did not provide a lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-outcome estimate. The DailyMed Clinical Considerations section discusses risks associated with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, including several obstetric and maternal outcomes; the returned extract does not establish that these outcomes were caused by lamotrigine. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The reviews describe pregnancy management as balancing maternal seizure control with fetal considerations. These are review-level discussions, not a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome study. [S19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/) [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

**Evidence gap:** Maternal lamotrigine-specific outcomes were not established in the retrieved extract. This is not evidence that such outcomes were absent or that the medicine is safe.

### 2. Maternal pharmacokinetics

#### Clinical Considerations

The selected label states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The label presents this as clinician-management information; no individualized dose or adjustment plan is provided here. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

#### Literature

- A pregnancy review states that physiological changes during pregnancy affect antiseizure-medication levels and seizure risk. The abstract does not provide numerical lamotrigine pharmacokinetic measurements. [S19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)
- A review specifically covering lamotrigine and other antiseizure medicines lists pharmacokinetics as a topic, but its retrieved abstract does not report numerical lamotrigine pregnancy pharmacokinetic results. [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33573557/)
- A naturalistic study of 60 mothers measured psychopharmacologic medications in serum and breastmilk at different time points during pregnancy and lactation and followed exposed children for the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine, but does not provide a lamotrigine-specific maternal serum concentration, clearance estimate, or fetal concentration. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

**Interpretation limit:** Candidate pharmacokinetic passages were retrieved, but human lamotrigine pregnancy pharmacokinetic data were not confirmed as a complete, drug-specific dataset in this extract. No administered regimen, dose estimate, or personal monitoring plan is provided.

### 3. Fetal exposure

No direct fetal lamotrigine concentration measurement was retrieved. The available material therefore describes maternal concentration changes and a breastmilk concentration ratio in a mixed-medication study, but does not quantify fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

A recruiting observational study is investigating antiseizure-medication clearance, physiological factors affecting blood concentrations in pregnant adults with epilepsy, and exposure to unborn children and nursing infants. Its registration and recruitment status indicate an investigation in progress, not posted fetal-exposure results. [S9](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05450978)

### 4. Fetal and infant outcomes

#### Human registry and epidemiologic findings

The selected label reports the following first-trimester lamotrigine-monotherapy registry findings:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** exposed infants, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 1.6%–3.1%.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** exposed infants.
- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9%** of **2,514** first-trimester exposures, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 2.3%–3.7%.

The label states that these registry data did not show an overall increased frequency or consistent pattern of major malformations, while also noting that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment, and comparator groups limit interpretation. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

For isolated oral clefts, the NAAED registry reported **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control analysis reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.8–2.63. These findings are not uniform across the cited sources. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It reports that the available data did not suggest increased risk of these outcomes with lamotrigine monotherapy, but explicitly limits the conclusions because outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups differed. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A naturalistic mixed-medication study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific outcome estimate, so this finding should not be treated as a standalone lamotrigine result. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

#### Animal findings

The label separately reports developmental findings in pregnant animals, including reduced fetal body weight, skeletal variations, neurobehavioral abnormalities, offspring mortality, and reduced fetal folate concentrations in rats. These are animal findings and are not fetal human outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### 5. FAERS report-only context

The returned FAERS query covered reports matching lamotrigine plus the reaction term “foetal exposure during pregnancy”; it was not a complete exposed population, and the source population was not established. Reported terms and counts included:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes. The returned FAERS interpretation states that causation and incidence cannot be established and that the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### 6. Gaps that remain visible

- No direct fetal lamotrigine concentration was retrieved.
- No numerical, lamotrigine-specific maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic dataset was retrieved in the abstracts.
- No lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-outcome estimate was retrieved.
- Registry findings vary for isolated oral clefts.
- The label identifies limitations involving outcome definitions, ascertainment, and comparator groups.
- The retrieved literature includes mixed indications and populations; findings should not be generalized beyond the populations actually described.
- The selected DailyMed label represents one product label rather than all lamotrigine formulations, and its general pregnancy text was truncated. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

- Does this evidence apply to the exact lamotrigine formulation and any other active ingredients?
- Which retrieved findings apply to the indication being treated—epilepsy, bipolar disorder, or another condition?
- How do the registry populations and exposure timing compare with the relevant pregnancy context?
- What maternal concentration or clinical-response information, if any, is appropriate to review during pregnancy and after delivery?
- Which findings represent measured exposure, and which represent observed fetal or infant outcomes?
- How should uncertainty about the conflicting oral-cleft findings be discussed?
- What are the risks of changing treatment, given that the MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medicine can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician?

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

| Observed outcomes in fetus or infant | 6 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 4 | 1 |
These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation: research summary\\n\\nSertraline was identity-matched as the ingredient sertraline. The lactation evidence below comes primarily from the retrieved LactMed record, revised August 15, 2026; its **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so this is not a complete record. [S45](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nThese are **milk measurements**, not infant outcomes or treatment instructions:\\n\\n- In pooled data from **15 mothers**, mean breastmilk sertraline concentration was **45 mcg/L** (range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**). [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a study of **26 women** averaging 15.8 weeks postpartum, mean milk concentrations were **129 mcg/L** for sertraline (range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**) and **258 mcg/L** for norsertraline (range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**), using extensive sampling over 24 hours. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In four mothers at 2 months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; samples were collected at random times. ## Sertraline during lactation: research summary

Sertraline was identity-matched as the ingredient sertraline. The lactation evidence below comes primarily from the retrieved LactMed record, revised August 15, 2026; its **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so this is not a complete record. [S45](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure

These are **milk measurements**, not infant outcomes or treatment instructions:

- In pooled data from **15 mothers**, mean breastmilk sertraline concentration was **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**). [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of **26 women** averaging 15.8 weeks postpartum, mean milk concentrations were **129 mcg/L** for sertraline (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and **258 mcg/L** for norsertraline (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**), using extensive sampling over 24 hours. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In four mothers at 2 months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; samples were collected at random times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one report involving a preterm infant, three random milk samples averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after administration contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In nine women providing trough samples during the first postpartum week, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman; the other eight had concentrations of **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**. LactMed notes that the timing of collection could affect these values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In six women providing random samples, the median concentration was **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**); LactMed notes that these values might be inaccurate because of sample timing. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 15 mothers providing repeated samples, mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**). [S42](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Infant-level measurements:** The retrieved LactMed extract states that norsertraline is often detectable at low levels in **infant serum**, but the detailed infant-level measurement passage was not returned. Thus, infant specimen results are incomplete in this extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The LactMed record reports:

- In **26 infants** in one study, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study. The source population was breastfed infants of mothers receiving sertraline; the design label was not stated in the returned passage. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of **14 mother–infant pairs**, no adverse effects were reported, including among six exclusively breastfed infants younger than 3 months. Infant whole-blood serotonin measurements were also reported; this was a measured biological outcome, not a milk concentration. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **25 infants** followed through 6 months, reported weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **six infants aged 5–34 weeks**, no clinical adverse reactions were noted at the time of the study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **seven 4-week-old infants**, no adverse effects were reported. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One **4-month-old infant** had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of infants of depressed mothers exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and breastfeeding, blunted pain responses were reported compared with infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers. Four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline. The returned passage states that there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, so an effect related to maternal depression or behavior could not be excluded. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- An uncontrolled online survey of **930 mothers** using antidepressants reported discontinuation-type symptoms in about 10% of infants; the finding was not sertraline-specific and included pregnancy as well as breastfeeding exposure. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a telephone study of mothers taking benzodiazepines while nursing, one mother also taking sertraline and other medicines reported sedation in her breastfed infant. Because of the co-exposures and the limited information returned, attribution to sertraline is not established. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

#### Separate case report

LactMed reports one case involving a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks**:

- The mother used sertraline during gestation, at delivery, and postpartum while exclusively breastfeeding.
- The infant developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation problems, and high-pitched crying during the first 24 hours; symptoms worsened on day 4 while breastfeeding continued.
- Breastfeeding was discontinued on day 9; the source reports that symptoms then dissipated and infant drug concentrations decreased.
- The infant was later found to have genetically intermediate metabolism of two CYP450 enzymes.
- The authors attributed the presentation to serotonergic overstimulation associated with persistent exposure through breastmilk and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report, not an incidence estimate. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Lactation and milk-production findings

These findings concern the lactating person or breastfeeding process, not direct infant toxicity:

- A report involving six people described decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the returned passage does not provide administered amounts, and the report was observational.
- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor exposure included only one sertraline-exposed participant and reported delayed onset of lactogenesis compared with controls; the returned passage states that there was no statistically significant difference in feeding difficulties after day 4.
- Other cited studies examined SSRI or antidepressant exposure during pregnancy or postpartum and breastfeeding outcomes, but several were not sertraline-specific and may be influenced by the underlying maternal condition.
