{"answer": "## Sertraline during lactation: research summary

Sertraline was identity-matched as the ingredient sertraline. The lactation evidence below comes primarily from the retrieved LactMed record, revised August 15, 2026; its **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so this is not a complete record. [S45](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure

These are **milk measurements**, not infant outcomes or treatment instructions:

- In pooled data from **15 mothers**, mean breastmilk sertraline concentration was **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**). [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of **26 women** averaging 15.8 weeks postpartum, mean milk concentrations were **129 mcg/L** for sertraline (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and **258 mcg/L** for norsertraline (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**), using extensive sampling over 24 hours. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In four mothers at 2 months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; samples were collected at random times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one report involving a preterm infant, three random milk samples averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after administration contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In nine women providing trough samples during the first postpartum week, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman; the other eight had concentrations of **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**. LactMed notes that the timing of collection could affect these values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In six women providing random samples, the median concentration was **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**); LactMed notes that these values might be inaccurate because of sample timing. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 15 mothers providing repeated samples, mean milk concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**). [S42](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38841362/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Infant-level measurements:** The retrieved LactMed extract states that norsertraline is often detectable at low levels in **infant serum**, but the detailed infant-level measurement passage was not returned. Thus, infant specimen results are incomplete in this extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

The LactMed record reports:

- In **26 infants** in one study, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study. The source population was breastfed infants of mothers receiving sertraline; the design label was not stated in the returned passage. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of **14 mother–infant pairs**, no adverse effects were reported, including among six exclusively breastfed infants younger than 3 months. Infant whole-blood serotonin measurements were also reported; this was a measured biological outcome, not a milk concentration. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **25 infants** followed through 6 months, reported weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **six infants aged 5–34 weeks**, no clinical adverse reactions were noted at the time of the study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In **seven 4-week-old infants**, no adverse effects were reported. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One **4-month-old infant** had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of infants of depressed mothers exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and breastfeeding, blunted pain responses were reported compared with infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers. Four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline. The returned passage states that there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, so an effect related to maternal depression or behavior could not be excluded. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- An uncontrolled online survey of **930 mothers** using antidepressants reported discontinuation-type symptoms in about 10% of infants; the finding was not sertraline-specific and included pregnancy as well as breastfeeding exposure. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a telephone study of mothers taking benzodiazepines while nursing, one mother also taking sertraline and other medicines reported sedation in her breastfed infant. Because of the co-exposures and the limited information returned, attribution to sertraline is not established. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

#### Separate case report

LactMed reports one case involving a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks**:

- The mother used sertraline during gestation, at delivery, and postpartum while exclusively breastfeeding.
- The infant developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation problems, and high-pitched crying during the first 24 hours; symptoms worsened on day 4 while breastfeeding continued.
- Breastfeeding was discontinued on day 9; the source reports that symptoms then dissipated and infant drug concentrations decreased.
- The infant was later found to have genetically intermediate metabolism of two CYP450 enzymes.
- The authors attributed the presentation to serotonergic overstimulation associated with persistent exposure through breastmilk and reduced metabolism. This is a single case report, not an incidence estimate. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These findings concern the lactating person or breastfeeding process, not direct infant toxicity:

- A report involving six people described decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the returned passage does not provide administered amounts, and the report was observational.
- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor exposure included only one sertraline-exposed participant and reported delayed onset of lactogenesis compared with controls; the returned passage states that there was no statistically significant difference in feeding difficulties after day 4.

Its pregnancy text was truncated in one field, although the structured PLLR 8.1 sections were returned. DailyMed states that in-use labeling may differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Maternal effects and underlying disease\\n\\nThe label states that most lamotrigine pregnancy data come from women with **epilepsy**. It separately describes pregnancy-associated risks reported with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These are presented as **underlying-disease and treatment-context risks**, not as lamotrigine-specific adverse effects. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe label also reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is source labeling for clinician discussion, not an individualized medication plan. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nA 2023 review of epilepsy in pregnancy and lactation states that pregnancy safety evidence in this population relies substantially on pregnancy registries, cohort studies, case-control studies, and prospective cohorts because large randomized safety trials have not been conducted. The source population is **pregnant women with epilepsy and lactation**, and the publication type is **review**. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)\\n\\n### Fetal or infant exposure\\n\\nNo numeric human fetal concentration was retrieved.\\n\\nA 2023 study of **60 mothers**, with source populations including **pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children**, measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at multiple time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high breastmilk concentration-to-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but does not provide a lamotrigine-specific milk concentration, fetal concentration, or infant-level concentration in the retrieved text. The study design label was not stated in the returned abstract metadata. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)\\n\\nThe label reports animal findings, including decreased fetal folate concentrations in rats and developmental findings in animals. These are **animal data**, not measured human fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Observed fetal and infant outcomes\\n\\nFor **lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester**, the label reports:\\n\\n- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** exposed infants; 95% CI **1.6%\u20133.1%**.\\n- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** exposed infants.\\n- EURAP registry: major birth defects in **2.9%** of **2,514** exposures; 95% CI **2.3%\u20133.7%**.\\n\\nThe label states that the frequency of major congenital malformations was similar to general-population estimates. The underlying registry populations and comparator methods differ, so these figures should not be treated as a single pooled estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n**Isolated oral clefts:** The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported oral clefts in **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy; 95% CI **1.4\u20136.3**, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. A European case-control study reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**; 95% CI **0.8\u20132.63**. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age outcomes, and neurodevelopmental delay. The retrieved extract does not establish a lamotrigine-specific effect estimate for each of these outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe 60-mother naturalistic study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between its in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborn groups and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. request.question: Summarize lamotrigine pregnancy evidence for a research discussion, retaining label context about underlying disease alongside adverse findings. Keep maternal effects, exposure and infant outcomes separate, with limitations and questions for the clinician. No treatment decisions.

response.answer:
## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

**Evidence scope:** Lamotrigine identity was verified. The retrieved evidence consists of one selected DailyMed product label plus a bounded PubMed search; it is not a systematic review. The DailyMed label is for one product/formulation, with effective date **October 12, 2026** and publication date **November 9, 2026**. Its pregnancy text was truncated in one field, although the structured PLLR 8.1 sections were returned. DailyMed states that in-use labeling may differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

The label states that most lamotrigine pregnancy data come from women with **epilepsy**. It separately describes pregnancy-associated risks reported with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These are presented as **underlying-disease and treatment-context risks**, not as lamotrigine-specific adverse effects. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is source labeling for clinician discussion, not an individualized medication plan. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A 2023 review of epilepsy in pregnancy and lactation states that pregnancy safety evidence in this population relies substantially on pregnancy registries, cohort studies, case-control studies, and prospective cohorts because large randomized safety trials have not been conducted. The source population is **pregnant women with epilepsy and lactation**, and the publication type is **review**. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

### Fetal or infant exposure

No numeric human fetal concentration was retrieved.

A 2023 study of **60 mothers**, with source populations including **pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children**, measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at multiple time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high breastmilk concentration-to-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but does not provide a lamotrigine-specific milk concentration, fetal concentration, or infant-level concentration in the retrieved text. The study design label was not stated in the returned abstract metadata. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The label reports animal findings, including decreased fetal folate concentrations in rats and developmental findings in animals. These are **animal data**, not measured human fetal exposure. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

For **lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester**, the label reports:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** exposed infants; 95% CI **1.6%–3.1%**.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** exposed infants.
- EURAP registry: major birth defects in **2.9%** of **2,514** exposures; 95% CI **2.3%–3.7%**.

The label states that the frequency of major congenital malformations was similar to general-population estimates. The underlying registry populations and comparator methods differ, so these figures should not be treated as a single pooled estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

**Isolated oral clefts:** The NAAED Pregnancy Registry reported oral clefts in **3.2 per 1,000** among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy; 95% CI **1.4–6.3**, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control study reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**; 95% CI **0.8–2.63**. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age outcomes, and neurodevelopmental delay. It also states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. The retrieved extract does not establish a lamotrigine-specific effect estimate for each of these outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The 60-mother naturalistic study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between its in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborn groups and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The abstract does not establish the lamotrigine-specific subgroup size or outcome estimates, so this finding should not be generalized to all lamotrigine-exposed pregnancies. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### FAERS report-only context

For the queried lamotrigine pregnancy-report subset, FAERS returned:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These are reporting volumes for reports matching the query, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or evidence of causation. The source states that exposure denominators were unavailable and that the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Limitations

- Most label pregnancy data are from women with epilepsy; applicability to bipolar disorder or another indication is not established by the retrieved extract. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Registry findings concern specific populations, exposure periods, and comparator groups; they should not be merged into one estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Monotherapy findings should not be generalized to polytherapy or unreported co-exposures. The retrieved label data specifically describe monotherapy for the registry percentages. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- One DailyMed pregnancy field was truncated; missing text is an extraction limitation, not evidence that additional information is absent. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- Seven requested PubMed records had abstract text retrieved, but the search was bounded and not a complete literature review. [S11](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- No curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed was identified in this MCP source review; pregnancy findings came from product labeling and primary literature, with non-exhaustive coverage. This is an MCP-generated coverage notice, not a claim that no such resource exists. [S28](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S29](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

### Questions for the clinician

1. Which evidence population best matches the underlying condition: epilepsy, bipolar disorder, or another indication?
2. Does the evidence apply to the exact formulation and any co-medications?
3. How should the isolated oral-cleft signal be interpreted given the differing registry findings and comparator groups?
4. Which outcome definitions and gestational periods are most relevant to the research question?
5. What human exposure measurements, if any, are available for the specific pregnancy or infant context?
6. How should the label’s reported pregnancy-related concentration changes be interpreted for the specific clinical context?
7. Would the North American Antiepileptic Drug Pregnancy Registry be relevant to the research discussion? The FDA directory lists it as ongoing, but the directory states that current enrollment should be verified directly. [S27](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries) [S26](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

The MCP server’s continuity-of-care notice: stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; such changes belong in discussion with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
